stories.title: Typhoon Noul Forces 20,000 People to Flee
stories.headline_kid: A giant spinning storm called Typhoon Noul is crashing into southern China, and more than 20,000 people had to leave their homes to stay safe.
summary: A typhoon is like a super-sized, spinning storm with fierce winds and heavy rain — much bigger and stronger than the thunderstorms we get in Singapore. Typhoon Noul is one of these giant storms, and it is heading straight for the coast between Hong Kong and Guangdong province in southern China.

Chinese authorities did not want to take any chances. They moved more than 20,000 people away from areas expected to get hit hardest, and stopped train services so no one would get stranded when the storm arrived.

The typhoon was expected to smash into land, called 'making landfall', sometime between Saturday evening and Sunday morning, bringing torrential rain and gale-force winds strong enough to knock down trees and signboards.

This matters to us in Singapore too. Many families travel to Hong Kong or nearby parts of China for holidays, and storms like this can delay or cancel flights. It's also a reminder that our region often gets hit by powerful storms, even though Singapore itself is lucky to be mostly typhoon-free.

lenses.me: If your family is planning a trip to Hong Kong or China, storms like this could mean checking flight updates before you fly.
lenses.family: Your family's holiday plans might need a backup plan if a typhoon is forecast at your destination.
lenses.friends: Classmates with relatives in Hong Kong or Guangdong might be extra worried and following the news closely.
lenses.nation: Singapore's weather service keeps an eye on storms like this because they can affect flights, shipping and even our own rainy weather patterns.
lenses.world: Scientists say typhoons are getting stronger as ocean waters warm up, so more countries need better plans to keep people safe.

stories.title: Movie Magic Turns Chinese Villages into Tourist Hotspots
stories.headline_kid: A hit Chinese movie called Dear You is sending tourists flocking to old villages — and many Singaporean families actually have roots there!
summary: A movie called Dear You has become a huge hit in China, and now people are travelling to see the real villages where it was filmed. These villages are in a region called Chaoshan, in eastern Guangdong province.

Chaoshan is special because it is the ancestral homeland of the Teochew people — and many Singaporeans are Teochew! If your grandparents or great-grandparents speak Teochew, chances are your family's roots trace back to this very region.

Tourists are now visiting old buildings and even taking photos with models of 'qiaopi' — these are old letters and money that overseas Chinese workers once sent back home to their families, kind of like an old-fashioned version of sending money to relatives today.

The sudden rush of visitors is exciting for these villages, bringing in business, but it also brings challenges. Villagers worry about protecting their old buildings from damage and keeping some privacy in their own homes, now that curious tourists are wandering through.

lenses.me: If your family speaks Teochew, this story is literally about where your ancestors came from!
lenses.family: Some families might get curious and plan a heritage trip to trace their roots back to Chaoshan.
lenses.friends: You could ask your friends which dialect group their families belong to — it makes for a fun class discussion.
lenses.nation: Singapore's Teochew community is a big part of our multicultural identity, seen in our food, temples and festivals.
lenses.world: It shows how a single movie can spark real changes in tourism and pride in a place's history.

stories.title: Ships Clash Again Near Disputed Reef That Matters to Singapore
stories.headline_kid: For the second day in a row, Chinese and Philippine ships have clashed near a disputed reef — and it matters to us because our shopping and food often sail through these same waters.
summary: The Philippines says Chinese coast guard ships fired water cannons at their government boats near Scarborough Shoal, a small reef in the South China Sea that both countries claim as their own. A water cannon is a powerful jet of water strong enough to knock people over or rock a boat dangerously.

This is the second day this has happened, and it's part of a bigger disagreement. Several countries, including China and the Philippines, claim different parts of the South China Sea, and their coast guard ships sometimes bump into each other there.

China's coast guard says it was just enforcing 'control measures' because it believes the Philippine ships were operating illegally in the area. The Philippines says its ships were doing nothing wrong.

Even though Singapore doesn't claim any of this territory, we care a lot about what happens there. Ships carrying our food, electronics, toys and fuel sail through the South China Sea every single day. If tensions rise too much, it could delay goods and raise prices for everyone here.

lenses.me: The toys, snacks and gadgets you use may have travelled through this very sea on a cargo ship.
lenses.family: If shipping gets disrupted, things your family buys could take longer to arrive or cost more.
lenses.friends: It's a good example of how events far away can still affect what happens in your own home.
lenses.nation: Singapore is a major trading port, so keeping sea routes peaceful and open is very important for our economy.
lenses.world: Disputes like this remind countries why they need rules and cooperation to avoid bigger conflicts at sea.

stories.title: Malaysia Aims to Make Its Own Vaccines by 2028
stories.headline_kid: Our neighbour Malaysia wants to make its own vaccines by 2028, instead of buying all of them from other countries.
summary: A vaccine is like a training exercise for your body's defence system — it teaches your immune system to recognise and fight off a germ before it can make you seriously sick. Right now, Malaysia has to buy almost all of its vaccines from other countries.

Malaysia's government has announced a plan to change this. By 2028, they hope to produce their very first locally-made vaccine, which will help protect people against illnesses like pneumonia, meningitis and blood infections.

This is a big deal because relying on other countries for vaccines can be risky. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many countries struggled to get enough vaccines quickly because supplies were limited and demand was sky-high everywhere at once.

Singapore, like Malaysia, imports most of its vaccines too. If our neighbours in the region can make their own, it could mean faster and more reliable vaccine supplies for everyone nearby during future health emergencies.

lenses.me: Vaccines you might get at school, like certain jabs, often come from factories overseas — this shows how that could change.
lenses.family: Steady vaccine supplies matter for keeping younger siblings and grandparents protected from serious illnesses.
lenses.friends: This connects to what you learn in science class about germs, immunity and how vaccines work.
lenses.nation: Singapore could benefit from working with Malaysia to make sure our region has enough vaccines during emergencies.
lenses.world: It shows a growing trend of countries wanting to make their own medicines instead of depending fully on others.

stories.title: She Sold Her House to Save Her Dream Restaurant
stories.headline_kid: Almost 30 years ago, Magdalene Tang sold her own house just to keep her Singapore restaurant alive — and today, Mag's is still going strong!
summary: Magdalene Tang opened a small wine bar on Circular Road in Singapore many years ago. When the business hit tough times, instead of giving up, she made a bold and brave choice — she sold her own house to keep her dream alive.

That wine bar eventually grew into Mag's, one of Singapore's longest-running independent restaurants. Over almost 30 years, Tang has guided the restaurant through several financial crises, changing food trends, and even the difficult years of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Through it all, she kept adapting — changing the menu, trying new ideas, and staying closely involved in every part of the restaurant, from the food to the wine to how guests are treated. Her tough, no-nonsense exterior hides a warm heart that truly loves making people feel welcome.
Mag's story shows how passion and perseverance can help a small business survive against the odds, becoming a beloved part of Singapore's food and dining scene.

lenses.me: It shows that even when something feels really hard, not giving up can lead to something amazing years later.
lenses.family: Your family might have a favourite old restaurant or hawker stall with a similar story of struggle and survival.
lenses.friends: You could chat with classmates about local food places that have been around for a long time.
lenses.nation: Stories like this are part of what makes Singapore's food scene so rich and full of history.
lenses.world: It's an example of how small businesses everywhere can survive tough global events, like the pandemic, through hard work and adapting.
